paper_id: Ni et al. - 2004 - LANDMARC Indoor Location Sensing Using Active RFID
title: LANDMARC: Indoor Location Sensing Using Active RFID
motivation: GPS fails indoors; existing indoor solutions (infrared, 802.11, ultrasonic) have line-of-sight, accuracy, or cost limitations.
problem_framing: Use cheap reference tags as calibration landmarks to compensate for RFID's lack of native signal strength reporting.
key_insight: Reference tags experiencing identical environmental effects as tracking tags enable relative signal-strength comparison for location estimation.
method_signature: k-nearest neighbor with inverse-square weighted Euclidean distance in signal-strength space
evaluation_criteria: Error distance (Euclidean) between computed and true coordinates; CDF of error at 50th and 90th percentiles
negative_result_or_admitted_limitation: Initial reader-placement approach fails because dynamic interference causes inconsistent detection ranges for static objects.
evidence_for_taste: Such a nicely formulated optimization problem turns out to be useless
the physical distance cannot be computed accurately by using power levels directly
the improvement is not as great as we expected
the accuracy has dropped quite significantly
the error due to the dynamics of the environment can hardly be alleviated
thinking_moves: Faced with environmental noise destroying distance-to-signal mapping, pivot to using redundant cheap sensors as relative landmarks
Formulate location as a k-nearest-neighbor lookup problem in signal-strength space rather than direct coordinate computation
Validate robustness by comparing daytime vs nighttime (high vs low interference) conditions
Identify cost-accuracy tradeoff: readers expensive, tags cheap; exploit many cheap tags over few expensive readers
